newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China mark stamped on HK business before handover.
newsitem.headline: China mark stamped on HK business before handover.

text.p: China may need to wait another 20 days to take control of Hong Kong, but in the business world its presence is already firmly felt in major industries and set to spread into the finance sector, analysts said on Wednesday.
"They are now involved in almost every segment of business here, terminals, telecoms and power," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International.
"It is important for China to see that the interests of Chinese and Hong Kong people are well taken care of."

Mainland interests laid their claim to Hong Kong's airlines during a major shakeup of the industry last year which saw the dominant British "hongs", or trading houses, lose some of their influence in the territory.

China-backed CITIC Pacific Ltd bolstered its stake in Cathay Pacific Airlines Ltd to control 25 percent of the Hong Kong flag carrier, while China National Aviation Corp bought 36 percent of Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd.
Colonial powerhouse Swire Pacific Ltd saw its holding reduced in both airlines.

"What China wants to do is illustrate that the old colonial hong theme is slowly dissipating and here comes the emergence of a new hong type," said Keith Wu, head of Hong Kong and China research at Peregrine Securities.
CITIC Pacific re-emerged this year to take a 20 percent stake in Hong Kong utility China Light & Power Co Ltd.
China rounded off its foray into Hong Kong business only last week by buying a 5.5 percent stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd, days before the territory reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
"There is perhaps no industry that is so strategic," said Fredson Bowers, director of Asia telecoms research at W.I. Carr.
Analysts said China may now be preparing its next move in Hong Kong's powerful financial sector.

"That is why you are seeing some of the smaller banks perform so well," said Wu. "Banks such as Ka Wah Bank, Union Bank as well as International Bank of Asia have been some of the top market performers recently."
HSBC Holdings Plc's subsidiary Hang Seng Bank Ltd is also cited as a likely target, although HSBC denies it has plans to sell a stake.
"We don't have this on our agenda. It has never been discussed on the board," Hongkong and Shanghai Bank executive director Vincent Cheng told Reuters in a recent interview.

While China may be seeking control some of the territory's major industries, analysts said that Hong Kong companies are also eager for ties with China in an effort to get more exposure to the mainland market.
"It is not just that the Chinese are desperately looking for equity participation. It's also the other way round," said Wu.

"The local (Hong Kong) market has limited growth potential and companies have to diversify. North of the border there is a major piece of pie and these local mature companies are trying to use their expertise to join hands with local China parties."
As China's influence grows, both as a shareholder and as a market, the Hong Kong stock market is set to broaden its base.

"The Hong Kong market is now blending its original, mature earnings base with this emerging market concept that the Chinese can offer," said Wu. "Chinese assets and liquidity will offer a deeper and broader base."
